warmup.q: Three consumer threads take from a BlockingQueue. When the producers are done, the coordinator puts ONE poison pill, and each consumer stops when it takes a pill. What happens?
options: All three consumers stop: they all see the pill
One consumer stops; the other two wait in take() forever
The queue throws, because a pill can only be taken once
Nothing stops until the queue is garbage collected
warmup.why: A pill is just an element: the first consumer to take it removes it from the queue and stops. The other two find an empty queue and wait in take() forever. Anything that joins the consumers, such as a shutdown hook, hangs too. You need one pill per consumer.

sections.h: Producer-consumer: a bounded queue between two speeds
sections.html:
Most of the concurrent code in a backend is this shape. Something produces work at one speed, such as a Kafka consumer polling records or request threads accepting payments, and something else processes it at another speed, such as a writer that inserts into Oracle. A BlockingQueue sits between them.

Bound the queue. A bounded queue is how a slow consumer pushes back on a fast producer: put waits when the queue is full, so the producer slows to the consumer's pace instead of filling memory. Lesson 9 of this track showed what the unbounded default does during an incident.

The hard part is stopping. Consumers wait in take(), and take() never returns on an empty queue. The standard answer is a poison pill: a special element that means "no more work". Three rules make it work:

  • Put the pills only after every producer has finished, so they land behind every real record.
  • Put one pill per consumer. A pill is taken once.
  • Compare against the pill by identity. A pill made with new String("PILL") is a unique object, so a real record that happens to read PILL is still a record.
Java
// consumer
while (true) {
    String record = queue.take();          // waits while the queue is empty
    if (record == PILL) break;             // identity: a record "PILL" is still a record
    settle(record);
}

// coordinator, after every producer has finished:
for (int i = 0; i < consumers; i++) queue.put(PILL);   // one pill per consumer
Kotlin
// consumer
while (true) {
    val record = queue.take()          // waits while the queue is empty
    if (record === PILL) break         // identity: a record "PILL" is still a record
    settle(record)
}

// coordinator, after every producer has finished:
repeat(consumers) { queue.put(PILL) }  // one pill per consumer

The figure shows the queue at shutdown: the last real records, then the pills. Each consumer drains records until it hits a pill, so no record is left behind and no consumer is left waiting.

There are other ways to stop: interrupt the consumers, or have them poll with a timeout and check a flag. Interrupting is fast but drops whatever is still queued. Polling adds latency and a flag to get right. Pills are the clean choice when every queued record must be processed. The lab builds the whole pipeline.

try.title: One pill per consumer, or not
steps: Read PoisonPills. Two producers put 1,000 records each into a queue of 4; three consumers take them. After the producers finish, main puts the pills.
Run it. Note how many records each consumer handled.
Run it with -Pargs=onepill. Predict how many consumers are still waiting after one second, and in which thread state.

code.title: PoisonPills.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * Two producers, three consumers, one bounded queue, shut down with poison pills. * Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per consumer. */ public class PoisonPills { @SuppressWarnings("StringOperationCanBeSimplified") static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // compared by identity public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean onePill = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("onepill"); BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); List<Thread> consumers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { int done = 0; try { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) break; // this consumer stops; the others keep going done++; } System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " got its pill after " + done + " records"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "consumer-" + c); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); consumers.add(t); } Thread[] producers = new Thread[2]; for (int p = 0; p < 2; p++) { int me = p; producers[p] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put("settle-" + me + "-" + i); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); producers[p].start(); } for (Thread t : producers) t.join(); // 1. every producer is done... for (int c = 0; c < (onePill ? 1 : consumers.size()); c++) queue.put(PILL); // 2. ...then one pill each for (Thread t : consumers) t.join(1_000); List<Thread> stuck = consumers.stream().filter(Thread::isAlive).toList(); System.out.println("consumers still waiting: " + stuck.size() + (stuck.isEmpty() ? "" : " (" + stuck.get(0).getState() + " in take)")); } }

alt.title: PoisonPills.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two producers, three consumers, one bounded queue, shut down with poison pills. // Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per consumer. private val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a fresh object: compared by identity fun main(args: Array<String>) { val onePill = args.firstOrNull() == "onepill" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<String>(4) val consumers = List(3) { c -> thread(isDaemon = true, name = "consumer-$c") { var done = 0 while (true) { val r = queue.take() if (r === PILL) break // this consumer stops; the others keep going done++ } println("${Thread.currentThread().name} got its pill after $done records") } } val producers = List(2) { me -> thread { repeat(1_000) { i -> queue.put("settle-$me-$i") } } } producers.forEach { it.join() } // 1. every producer is done... repeat(if (onePill) 1 else consumers.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 2. ...then one pill each consumers.forEach { it.join(1_000) } val stuck = consumers.count { it.isAlive } println("consumers still waiting: $stuck" + if (stuck > 0) " (${consumers.last { it.isAlive }.state} in take)" else "") }

try.expect: With one pill each, all three consumers report their pill, their counts add up to 2,000, and consumers still waiting: 0. The split changes from run to run. With onepill, one consumer stops and two are still waiting: consumers still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take). In a real service, that is a shutdown that never finishes.

sections.h: Dining philosophers: five threads, five locks, one cycle
sections.html:
Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs both neighbouring forks. Each one picks up the left fork, then the right.

It works most of the time. Then, one day, all five pick up their left fork at the same moment. Each now waits for the right fork, which the next philosopher holds as a left fork. Nobody puts a fork down. That is the deadlock from lesson 6 of this track, with five locks instead of two: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait around the table. It is also what transfers look like when each one locks two of many accounts.

The simulator has three philosophers. Let them eat one at a time, then reset and give each one a single step first.

There are two standard fixes, and each removes a different condition.

Resource ordering removes the circular wait. Number the forks and always take the lower-numbered one first. Philosophers 0 to 3 still take left then right, but philosopher 4 needs forks 4 and 0, so it takes fork 0 first. The cycle can't close.

Java
int left = seat, right = (seat + 1) % n;
ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)];    // the last philosopher reaches right first
ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(left, right)];
Kotlin
val left = seat
val right = (seat + 1) % n
val first = forks[minOf(left, right)]     // the last philosopher reaches right first
val second = forks[maxOf(left, right)]

A waiter removes the chance that everyone holds one fork. Only four of the five may sit down at once, so at least one seated philosopher can always get both forks. A Semaphore(n - 1) is the waiter:

Java
seats.acquire();                 // Semaphore(n - 1): one chair short, so someone can always eat
try { eatWithBothForks(); } finally { seats.release(); }
Kotlin
seats.acquire()                 // Semaphore(n - 1): one chair short, so someone can always eat
try { eatWithBothForks() } finally { seats.release() }

A third fix, tryLock on the second fork with a random back-off, removes no-preemption, but brings back the livelock risk from lesson 6. Ordering is the one to use when you can number your resources. The waiter fits when you can't, or when you want to cap how many workers compete at all.

sim.title: Three philosophers, three forks, left first
sim.intro: Each philosopher takes the left fork, then the right one. First let them eat one at a time. Then reset and give each philosopher exactly one step before anyone takes a second.

goal.say: All three ate, one after another. Now reset and let each philosopher pick up a left fork first: every fork is held, every philosopher waits for the next one's fork, and the table freezes.

try.title: Freeze the table, then fix it two ways
steps: Read Philosophers. Five philosophers try to eat 200 meals each, pausing 1 ms between their two forks. After 3 seconds, the demo asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked.
Run it as is. Then run it with -Pargs=ordered and with -Pargs=waiter.
Compare the meal counts, the times and the deadlock count.

code.title: Philosophers.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), * with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). */ public class Philosophers { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "naive"; int n = 5; ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(); Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(n - 1); // the waiter: one chair short AtomicInteger meals = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] ps = new Thread[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int left = i, right = (i + 1) % n; int first = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.min(left, right) : left; int second = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.max(left, right) : right; ps[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int m = 0; m < 200; m++) { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.acquire(); try { forks[first].lock(); try { Thread.sleep(1); // reach for the other fork forks[second].lock(); try { meals.incrementAndGet(); } finally { forks[second].unlock(); } } finally { forks[first].unlock(); } } finally { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.release(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "philosopher-" + i); ps[i].setDaemon(true); ps[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L; // 3 s for the whole table for (Thread p : ps) p.join(Math.max(1, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)); long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.printf("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d%n", mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck == null ? 0 : stuck.length); } }

alt.title: Philosophers.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), // with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "naive" val n = 5 val forks = Array(n) { ReentrantLock() } val seats = Semaphore(n - 1) // the waiter: one chair short val meals = AtomicInteger() val ps = List(n) { i -> val left = i val right = (i + 1) % n val first = if (mode == "ordered") minOf(left, right) else left val second = if (mode == "ordered") maxOf(left, right) else right thread(isDaemon = true, name = "philosopher-$i") { repeat(200) { if (mode == "waiter") seats.acquire() try { forks[first].withLock { Thread.sleep(1) // reach for the other fork forks[second].withLock { meals.incrementAndGet() } } } finally { if (mode == "waiter") seats.release() } } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L // 3 s for the whole table ps.forEach { it.join(maxOf(1L, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d" .format(mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck?.size ?: 0)) }

try.expect: As is: almost no meals (0 or 1 in runs here) and deadlocked philosophers: 5, found by ThreadMXBean because the forks are ReentrantLocks. Ordered and waiter: all 1,000 meals in about a second, and deadlocked philosophers: 0 (the waiter version was slightly faster in runs here).

sections.html:
Many threads read a shared table and a few write it: BIN ranges read on every payment, refreshed once an hour. Readers can share; a writer needs the table to itself. The question is what happens when both are waiting, and each answer starves somebody.

Readers first lets a new reader in whenever no writer is inside. With a steady stream of overlapping readers, the reader count never drops to zero, so the writer never gets in. The refresh starves.

Writers first makes new readers wait as soon as a writer is waiting. The refresh gets in quickly, but under a stream of writers, readers starve.

A fair policy serves threads in arrival order. Nobody starves, and throughput drops, because readers that could have shared now wait behind a writer that arrived first.

The JDK's ReentrantReadWriteLock picks a middle path. In its default non-fair mode it doesn't promise an order, but a thread that asks for the read lock waits if the thread at the head of the queue wants to write. In practice that keeps a writer from being starved by a stream of new readers. Fair mode gives strict arrival order:

Java
new ReentrantReadWriteLock();        // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line
new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true);    // fair: strict arrival order, lower throughput
Kotlin
ReentrantReadWriteLock()        // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line
ReentrantReadWriteLock(true)    // fair: strict arrival order, lower throughput

The Try it shows the difference. A textbook readers-first lock, written with synchronized, makes a writer wait as long as the readers keep coming, while ReentrantReadWriteLock lets it in within a couple of milliseconds.

Before choosing a policy, ask whether readers need a lock at all. If the writer replaces the whole table, the snapshot pattern from lesson 11 of this track lets readers read an immutable map with no lock and no waiting, and the question of who starves goes away. Oracle takes the same approach with multiversion reads: readers see a consistent older version and don't wait for writers.

try.title: Starve a writer
steps: Read ReadersWriters. Four readers hold the lock for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for 1.5 seconds. 100 ms in, one writer asks for the lock. The demo measures how long it waits, first with a hand-written readers-first lock, then with ReentrantReadWriteLock.

code.title: ReadersWriters.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * Four readers keep a rate table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. * How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? */ public class ReadersWriters { interface RW { void readLock() throws InterruptedException; void readUnlock(); void writeLock() throws InterruptedException; void writeUnlock(); } /** The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. */ static final class ReadersFirst implements RW { private int readers; private boolean writing; public synchronized void readLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing) wait(); readers++; } public synchronized void readUnlock() { if (--readers == 0) notifyAll(); } public synchronized void writeLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing || readers > 0) wait(); writing = true; } public synchronized void writeUnlock() { writing = false; notifyAll(); } } static final class Jdk implements RW { private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); public void readLock() { rw.readLock().lock(); } public void readUnlock() { rw.readLock().unlock(); } public void writeLock() { rw.writeLock().lock(); } public void writeUnlock() { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } static long writerWaitMs(RW lock) throws InterruptedException { long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L; Thread[] readers = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < readers.length; i++) { readers[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock(); try { Thread.sleep(2); } finally { lock.readUnlock(); } // a 2 ms read } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); readers[i].start(); Thread.sleep(1); // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); lock.writeLock(); // the refresh wants in long waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; lock.writeUnlock(); for (Thread r : readers) r.join(); return waited; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("readers-first lock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new ReadersFirst()) + " ms"); System.out.println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new Jdk()) + " ms"); } }

alt.title: ReadersWriters.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Four readers keep a rate table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. // How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? private interface RwLock { fun readLock(); fun readUnlock(); fun writeLock(); fun writeUnlock() } // The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. private class ReadersFirst : RwLock { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() private var readers = 0 private var writing = false override fun readLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing) changed.await(); readers++ } } override fun readUnlock() { lock.withLock { if (--readers == 0) changed.signalAll() } } override fun writeLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing || readers > 0) changed.await(); writing = true } } override fun writeUnlock() { lock.withLock { writing = false; changed.signalAll() } } } private class Jdk : RwLock { private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() override fun readLock() = rw.readLock().lock() override fun readUnlock() = rw.readLock().unlock() override fun writeLock() = rw.writeLock().lock() override fun writeUnlock() = rw.writeLock().unlock() } private fun writerWaitMs(lock: RwLock): Long { val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L val readers = List(4) { thread { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock() try { Thread.sleep(2) } finally { lock.readUnlock() } // a 2 ms read } }.also { Thread.sleep(1) } // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100) val t0 = System.nanoTime() lock.writeLock() // the refresh wants in val waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 lock.writeUnlock() readers.forEach { it.join() } return waited } fun main() { println("readers-first lock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(ReadersFirst())} ms") println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(Jdk())} ms") }

try.expect: Readers-first: the writer waits about 1,400 ms, until the readers stop on their own. ReentrantReadWriteLock: about 1 to 2 ms, because new readers queue behind the waiting writer instead of overtaking it.

refs.title: jcstress samples, including Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem

analogy: Producer-consumer is a kitchen pass: cooks put plates on a shelf with room for eight, and waiters take them. When the shelf is full the cooks wait, and at closing time the head chef puts one "kitchen closed" card on the shelf for each waiter. Dining philosophers is five people sharing five chopsticks; numbering the chopsticks and always grabbing the lower number first stops the standoff. Readers-writers is a museum room: visitors can share it, but the restorer needs it empty, and someone has to decide whether new visitors may keep walking in while the restorer waits at the door. The analogy breaks at the closing card: a waiter who finds it would tell the others. A consumer that takes a pill just stops, and the other consumers learn nothing.
world: The Kafka-to-Oracle path in a payment service is producer-consumer: a poll loop produces records, a worker pool settles them, and a bounded queue between them is what keeps a slow database from turning into an out-of-memory crash. Shutdown is where it usually goes wrong. On SIGTERM the application gets a grace period (30 seconds by default in Kubernetes), and the pipeline has to stop polling, drain what is queued, commit offsets for what it finished, and stop. The worked example shows that order. Dining philosophers is any job that locks several resources at once: transfers that lock two accounts, a netting run that locks a merchant and a settlement batch. Readers-writers is every reference table you refresh while serving traffic.
mistake: The most common mistake is getting the poison pills wrong at shutdown: putting a single pill for several consumers, or putting the pills before every producer has finished. With one pill, the other consumers wait in take() forever and the shutdown hangs until the platform kills the pod, so whatever they were holding is lost. With pills sent too early, consumers stop while producers are still putting, the bounded queue fills, and the producers block forever instead. Both bugs pass every test that never shuts the pipeline down. The fix is the order in this lesson: stop the producers, join them, put one pill per consumer, then join the consumers with a deadline.

compare.title: Stopping consumers: pills in Java, a closed channel in Kotlin coroutines

java.title: Java, BlockingQueue
java.html: for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { pool.add(start(() -> { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) return; // each consumer needs its own pill settle(r); } })); } for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) queue.put(PILL); // 4 consumers, 4 pills for (Thread c : pool) c.join();

kotlin.title: Kotlin, kotlinx.coroutines Channel
kotlin.html: // a Channel can be closed, so there are no pills coroutineScope { val records = Channel<String>(capacity = 8) val producers = sources.map { src -> launch { for (r in src) records.send(r) } } repeat(4) { launch { for (r in records) settle(r) } } // each loop ends when the channel is closed AND empty producers.joinAll() records.close() // "no more records": consumers drain, then stop }

compare.note: With threads and a BlockingQueue, Kotlin code looks just like the Java version: the queue has no notion of "closed", so you still need one pill per consumer, compared with ===. The real difference comes with coroutines. A Channel can be closed: close() means no more elements, and every for (r in records) loop ends once the channel is closed and empty, however many consumers there are. That removes the whole class of pill-counting bugs. coroutineScope also waits for every consumer it launched, so there is no join loop to forget. The coroutines track covers channels properly.

worked.title: Shut a Kafka-to-database pipeline down without losing records

steps.say: A pipeline polls Kafka on two producer threads and settles records on four consumer threads, through a bounded queue. On SIGTERM, someone wrote this. What happens to the records already in the queue, and to the batch a consumer is halfway through?
steps.code: void shutdown() { for (Thread c : consumers) c.interrupt(); // stop now, whatever is in the queue for (Thread p : producers) p.interrupt(); }

alt.html: fun shutdown() { consumers.forEach { it.interrupt() } // stop now, whatever is in the queue producers.forEach { it.interrupt() } }

steps.say: Interrupting a consumer that waits in take() stops it at once, so everything still queued is dropped. A consumer in the middle of a database call may abort it halfway. And a producer may have polled records it never put. Because offsets were committed only for processed records, Kafka will redeliver what was lost, but the shutdown did a lot of work for nothing, and only idempotent settlement (lesson 3 of this track) keeps the redelivery safe.
The orderly version, with subgoal labels. running is a volatile flag the producers check in their poll loops.
steps.code: void shutdown() throws InterruptedException { running = false; // 1. producers stop polling Kafka for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); // 2. wait until no producer can put again for (int i = 0; i < consumers.size(); i++) { queue.put(PILL); // 3. one pill per consumer, behind every real record } long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30); for (Thread c : consumers) { c.join(Math.max(1, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))); // 4. one deadline for all } for (Thread c : consumers) if (c.isAlive()) c.interrupt(); // 5. still busy: interrupt; Kafka redelivers }

alt.html: fun shutdown() { running = false // 1. producers stop polling Kafka producers.forEach { it.join() } // 2. wait until no producer can put again repeat(consumers.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 3. one pill per consumer, behind every real record val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30) for (c in consumers) { c.join(maxOf(1L, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))) // 4. one deadline for all } consumers.filter { it.isAlive }.forEach { it.interrupt() } // 5. still busy: interrupt; Kafka redelivers }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself: why must step 2 finish before step 3 starts? Answer: a pill put while a producer is still running can land in front of that producer's last records. A consumer that takes the pill stops; with all consumers stopped and the queue bounded, the producer then blocks in put forever, and the shutdown hangs on step 2 of the next attempt. Joining the producers first guarantees that every real record is already ahead of the pills.

Step 5 is the safety net. If the database is down, the consumers can't drain the queue within the grace period. Interrupting them is then the right call: the records they didn't finish were never committed to Kafka, so another instance will process them after a rebalance. Orderly shutdown and idempotent processing work together; neither is enough alone.

lab.title: A pipeline that stops cleanly, and a table that can't deadlock
steps: Run the tests. All six fail. The three pipeline tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. The three DiningTable tests time out after 15 seconds: the philosophers deadlocked.

Part 1: write SettlementPipeline.run. Create an ArrayBlockingQueue of capacity and a unique pill (new String("PILL")). Start the consumers: each loops on take(), stops at the pill (compared with ==), and otherwise calls process and counts.
Start one producer thread per inner list. Join all producers, then put one pill per consumer, then join all consumers, then return the count.
Part 2: fix DiningTable.dine so every philosopher takes the lower-numbered fork first. Keep reachForTheOtherFork() between the two forks.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Count processed records with an AtomicInteger: several consumers increment it at once.
The second pipeline test checks that process is never called after run returns. If it fails, you return before joining every consumer.

For the table, compute a = seat and b = (seat + 1) % seats, then lock forks[min(a, b)] before forks[max(a, b)]. Only the last philosopher's order actually changes, and that is enough to break the cycle.
lab.done: All six tests in ClassicProblemsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Poison-pill shutdown from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Given started-but-not-yet-running producer and consumer threads and their shared BlockingQueue<String>, write the coordinator that runs the pipeline to completion with poison pills, plus the consumer's loop. Check: when are the pills put, how many, and how does a consumer recognize one?

answer.html: static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // a unique object, compared by identity static void runPipeline(List<Thread> producers, List<Thread> consumers, BlockingQueue<String> queue) throws InterruptedException { for (Thread c : consumers) c.start(); for (Thread p : producers) p.start(); for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); // every record is in the queue for (Thread c : consumers) queue.put(PILL); // one pill each, behind the records for (Thread c : consumers) c.join(); } // each consumer's loop: // while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) return; settle(r); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a unique object, compared by identity fun runPipeline(producers: List<Thread>, consumers: List<Thread>, queue: BlockingQueue<String>) { consumers.forEach { it.start() } producers.forEach { it.start() } producers.forEach { it.join() } // every record is in the queue consumers.forEach { queue.put(PILL) } // one pill each, behind the records consumers.forEach { it.join() } } // each consumer's loop: // while (true) { val r = queue.take(); if (r === PILL) return; settle(r) }

recap: Producer-consumer: a bounded BlockingQueue between two speeds; put waiting on a full queue is back-pressure.
Poison pills: put them only after every producer has finished, one per consumer, and compare by identity.
Dining philosophers is a circular wait. Take resources in one global order, or limit the competitors to n - 1 with a semaphore.
Readers-first starves writers, writers-first starves readers, fair order starves no one and costs throughput.
ReentrantReadWriteLock makes new readers wait behind a queued writer; fair mode gives strict arrival order.
If writers replace the whole table, an immutable snapshot removes the readers-writers problem entirely.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate how you would shut down a pipeline of 2 producers and 4 consumers so that no queued record is lost and no thread is left waiting.
explain.answer: First stop the producers from taking new work and wait for them to finish, so every real record is already in the queue. Then put four poison pills, one per consumer, behind those records. Each consumer keeps taking records until it takes a pill, so the queue drains completely and each one stops exactly once. The pill is a unique object compared with ==, so no real record can look like one. Finally, join the consumers with an overall deadline, and interrupt any that are still busy when it passes; whatever they didn't finish was never acknowledged, so it will be redelivered and must be processed idempotently.

deeper.html:
Poison pills are one of several ways to stop consumers. Executors use interruption: shutdownNow() interrupts every worker, and tasks are expected to stop when interrupted, as lesson 2 of this track described. A poll(timeout) loop that checks a volatile flag is simple but makes shutdown wait for up to one timeout, and adds a flag that every loop must check. Kotlin channels and reactive streams have completion built in, which is why they need no pills. Kafka's own consumer has wakeup(), which makes a blocked poll() throw WakeupException, the usual way to stop a poll loop from another thread.

The dining philosophers problem has more solutions than the two here. Chandy and Misra's solution passes "dirty" and "clean" forks between neighbours with requests, which avoids both deadlock and starvation and works across machines, at the cost of messages. A plain tryLock with back-off works, but needs randomness to avoid livelock. All of them are ways of removing one of the four conditions from lesson 6.

Readers-writers shows up all over databases. Oracle uses multiversion read consistency: a query reads the version of each block as of when the query started, so readers don't wait for writers and writers don't wait for readers. That is the immutable-snapshot idea from lesson 11 applied to storage, and it's why the problem rarely appears at the SQL level. Writers still wait for other writers on the same rows.

If you want to see these problems under a real stress harness, the jcstress samples include Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem. The next lesson shows how to run jcstress and read its results.
